newsitem.title: UK: UK pay plan threatens govt spending targets-papers.
newsitem.headline: UK pay plan threatens govt spending targets-papers.

text.p: An unexpectedly large pay rise for Britain's public sector workers could threaten the government's tight spending targets, newspapers reported on Friday.
Five independent pay review bodies have recommended doctors, teachers and the armed forces receive pay rises of between 3.2 and 3.4 percent, the Financial Times said on Friday.
The Guardian newspaper said Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke is preparing to phase in the awards in stages, gambling that workers will be assuaged by the relatively high overall increase.
Clarke is conscious of the need to ease the pressure on tight budgets, particularly in the health service, and may stagger the pay awards as a result, the Guardian said.
The FT said the pay rises were well above what could be accommodated by the government's public spending ceilings.
The cabinet is expected to discuss the pay round next week. A Treasury spokesman declined to comment on the reports, as did opposition Labour Party environment spokesman Frank Dobson.
"The whole object of those...leaks is to try to embarrass Labour so that somebody can be trapped into saying something daft," he told BBC radio.
Bob Abberley, health section head of the public sector union Unison said the government should implement whatever the pay review bodies recommended and introduce it in one go.
But Philip Hunt, director of the National Association of Health Authorities and Trusts, said the NHS could ill afford to meet the recommended pay increases.

"I don't think the health service can afford to pay 3.3, 3.4 percent," he said on the BBC's Today programme. "We've been allowed two percent for inflation in the allocation for health services next year. Any money higher than that figure will have to come out of the money we would want to spend on services."
It would be difficult, politically, for the government to reject the recommendations of the review boards outright in the run-up to an election which must be held by May.
Indeed, there will be a strong temptation to award the annual rises in full with the latest poll from the MORI organisation showing the opposition Labour Party revelling in a 25 point lead.
But the Guardian said Clarke will argue that staggering the pay awards will put the focus on the opposition Labour Party.

Shadow finance minister Gordon Brown has pledged to match the government's spending targets for two years if Labour comes to power but may come under extra pressure to implement the public sector pay rises without delay.
